title: OpenAI releases GPT-4, a multimodal AI that it claims is state-of-the-art
author: Kyle Wiggers

dom.t: Legal workflows: Immediate gains create competence risks

mo.t: AI competition: Distribution and habits rival capability
AI infrastructure: Scale advantages need not create monopoly
AI services: Deployment gaps create consulting opportunity
Generative automation: Fluent work product still needs authority
Legal workflows: Immediate gains create competence risks

kp.k: GPT-4 substantially improves simulated bar examination performance
kp.d: The article reports that GPT-4 performs at “human level” on various professional and academic benchmarks, including a simulated bar examination score around the top 10% of test takers, compared with GPT-3.5 around the bottom 10%. The reported result concerns benchmark performance, rather than evidence of performance in legal practice.
qs: For example, GPT-4 passes a simulated bar exam with a score around the top 10% of test takers; in contrast, GPT-3.5’s score was around the bottom 10%.

kp.k: Launch access combines paid subscriptions and metered API pricing
kp.d: At the March 14, 2023 launch, the article reports availability to ChatGPT Plus subscribers subject to a usage cap, with developers able to join an API waitlist. Reported pricing distinguishes input from generated output: $0.03 per 1,000 prompt tokens and $0.06 per 1,000 completion tokens, each described as about 750 words.
qs: Pricing is $0.03 per 1,000 “prompt” tokens (about 750 words) and $0.06 per 1,000 “completion” tokens (again, about 750 words).

kp.k: Multimodality extends AI assistance to image interpretation
kp.d: GPT-4 accepts images and text and generates text, whereas GPT-3.5 accepted only text. The article describes image captioning and interpretation, including identifying a Lightning Cable adapter. Image understanding was initially being tested with Be My Eyes rather than offered to all customers; that company's Virtual Volunteer description envisages identifying refrigerator contents, suggesting recipes and providing preparation instructions.
qs: GPT-4 can caption — and even interpret — relatively complex images, for example identifying a Lightning Cable adapter from a picture of a plugged-in iPhone.
The image understanding capability isn’t available to all OpenAI customers just yet — OpenAI’s testing it with a single partner, Be My Eyes, to start with.
Powered by GPT-4, Be My Eyes’ new Virtual Volunteer feature can answer questions about images sent to it.

kp.k: Early applications span support, education and financial knowledge retrieval
kp.d: The article reports GPT-4 deployment in Bing Chat and early adoption across other domains: Stripe for website summaries used by customer support staff, Duolingo for a language-learning subscription tier, Morgan Stanley for a system under development to retrieve company-document information for financial analysts, and Khan Academy for an automated tutor. These examples distinguish existing integrations from systems being developed; they are not reports of legal-service deployments.
qs: Morgan Stanley is creating a GPT-4-powered system that’ll retrieve info from company documents and serve it up to financial analysts.
And Khan Academy is leveraging GPT-4 to build some sort of automated tutor.

kp.k: System messages let developers prescribe behavior and boundaries
kp.d: Wiggers identifies steerability tooling as potentially a more meaningful improvement than image understanding. The new API system-message capability allows developers to specify style and task instructions and establish interaction boundaries. The article illustrates this with a Socratic tutor instructed to guide students through questions rather than provide answers, and reports that system messages would also come to ChatGPT.
qs: A more meaningful improvement in GPT-4, potentially, is the aforementioned steerability tooling.
With GPT-4, OpenAI is introducing a new API capability, “system” messages, that allow developers to prescribe style and task by describing specific directions.

kp.k: OpenAI attributes improvements to alignment and training infrastructure
kp.d: OpenAI says six months of iterative alignment, informed by internal adversarial testing and ChatGPT, produced its best results on factuality, steerability and guardrail adherence. The article reports training on publicly available and licensed data using an Azure supercomputer developed with Microsoft. OpenAI characterizes the advantage over GPT-3.5 as more apparent on sufficiently complex tasks than in casual conversation; these are company claims.
qs: OpenAI spent six months “iteratively aligning” GPT-4 using lessons from an internal adversarial testing program as well as ChatGPT, resulting in “best-ever results” on factuality, steerability and refusing to go outside of guardrails, according to the company.
Like previous GPT models, GPT-4 was trained using publicly available data, including from public webpages, as well as data that OpenAI licensed.
The difference comes out when the complexity of the task reaches a sufficient threshold — GPT-4 is more reliable, creative and able to handle much more nuanced instructions than GPT-3.5.

kp.k: Hallucinations and reasoning limitations persist despite improvements
kp.d: OpenAI acknowledges that GPT-4 still fabricates facts and makes confident reasoning errors. Its stated limitations include knowledge largely bounded by a September 2021 data cutoff, inability to learn from experience, acceptance of obvious falsehoods supplied by users and generation of code with security vulnerabilities. The article cites an erroneous description of Elvis Presley as the son of an actor.
qs: It still “hallucinates” facts and makes reasoning errors, sometimes with great confidence.
“GPT-4 generally lacks knowledge of events that have occurred after the vast majority of its data cuts off (September 2021), and does not learn from its experience,” OpenAI wrote.
It can sometimes make simple reasoning errors which do not seem to comport with competence across so many domains, or be overly gullible in accepting obvious false statements from a user.
And sometimes it can fail at hard problems the same way humans do, such as introducing security vulnerabilities into code it produces.

kp.d: The article attributes to OpenAI claims that GPT-4 is 82% less likely than GPT-3.5 to respond to requests for disallowed content and follows company policies on sensitive requests 29% more often. Separately, the article states that GPT-4 is less likely to refuse requests about synthesizing dangerous chemicals. These statements are reported as written, without reconciling that example with the aggregate safety claim.
qs: OpenAI does note, though, that it made improvements in particular areas; GPT-4 is less likely to refuse requests on how to synthesize dangerous chemicals, for one.

The company says that GPT-4 is 82% less likely overall to respond to requests for “disallowed” content compared to GPT-3.5 and responds to sensitive requests — e.g. medical advice and anything pertaining to self-harm — in accordance with OpenAI’s policies 29% more often.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Wiggers reports GPT-4’s expanded multimodal capabilities, stronger benchmark performance and emerging applications across customer support, education, finance and accessibility; he does not predict changes to legal employment or legal-service markets.
pts.d: This is a cross-domain product-release report. Wiggers reports that GPT-4 accepts images and text and generates text, and that it scores around the top 10% on a simulated bar exam versus GPT-3.5’s bottom 10%. This is a benchmark claim, not a claim that GPT-4 can replace practising lawyers. He describes Stripe using it for website summaries for customer support, Duolingo incorporating it into language learning, Morgan Stanley developing document retrieval for financial analysts, Khan Academy building an automated tutor, and Be My Eyes testing image-based assistance. Wiggers presents steerability through system messages as a potentially more meaningful improvement, allowing developers to prescribe style and task. The article attributes greater reliability on complex tasks and broader hoped-for benefits to OpenAI, rather than presenting these as independently established findings.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence consists primarily of reported benchmark results, OpenAI’s own testing claims, named adopter examples and illustrative capabilities or errors.
pts.d: Wiggers cites simulated bar-exam performance and other professional and academic benchmarks without supplying their detailed methods or independent validation. He reports OpenAI’s six-month alignment effort and its claimed improvements in factuality, steerability and guardrail adherence. OpenAI’s reported safety comparisons are an 82% lower likelihood of responding to disallowed requests and 29% more frequent policy-aligned responses to sensitive requests relative to GPT-3.5. Named deployments and development projects illustrate applications rather than measured productivity gains. Image interpretation examples and Be My Eyes’ described refrigerator-to-recipe functionality illustrate proposed capabilities. The Elvis Presley error supplies a concrete example of continuing factual unreliability. The article offers no study of legal practice, lawyer productivity or legal-market outcomes.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The claims concern the March 14, 2023 launch, with restricted initial access, applications at different development stages and explicit reliability limitations.
pts.d: At publication, GPT-4 was available to ChatGPT Plus users with a usage cap, while developers could join an API waitlist. Image understanding was initially being tested with Be My Eyes rather than made generally available. Morgan Stanley’s retrieval system and Khan Academy’s tutor were described as under development. System messages were introduced for the API, with future ChatGPT availability mentioned but no firm date stated. OpenAI qualified its comparison with GPT-3.5 by saying differences become clearer on sufficiently complex tasks. The article stresses continuing hallucinations, confident reasoning errors, a September 2021 cutoff for the vast majority of training data and lack of learning from experience. Broad benefits are presented as aspirations, not time-bound outcome forecasts.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: Affected groups include paying chatbot users, developers, customer-support staff, financial analysts, learners and visually impaired users.
pts.d: Paying ChatGPT users gain access to the new model subject to limits. Developers gain prospective API access and tools to specify model behaviour, with reported pricing of $0.03 per 1,000 prompt tokens and $0.06 per 1,000 completion tokens. Customer-support staff receive website summaries; financial analysts are intended to receive information retrieved from company documents; learners receive language-learning features or prospective automated tutoring. Be My Eyes users are offered image-question answering through its Virtual Volunteer feature, framed as assistance for visually impaired people. These examples concern assistance or task automation, not demonstrated elimination of professional roles. Although bar-exam takers provide a benchmark comparison, the article identifies no specific effects on lawyers, law firms, legal clients or access to justice.
